predecessors.name: Han dynasty
predecessors.text: Tượng Lâm (Xianglin) county of the Han Rinan commandery, 'modern-day Huế city', where Khu Liên's rising of 192 succeeded

successors.name: Đại Việt (Ngô to Hồ dynasties)
successors.text: Địa Lý, Ma Linh and Bố Chính (1069) and Ô and Lý (1306): Quảng Bình, Quảng Trị and Thừa Thiên

successors.name: Lê dynasty
successors.text: 'Northern Champa (now Quảng Nam, Quảng Ngãi and north of Phú Yên)': the land between the Hải Vân and Cù Mông passes

successors.name: Nguyễn lords
successors.text: Phú Yên (1611) and Kauthara, today Khánh Hòa (1653)

successors.name: Nguyễn dynasty (Đại Nam)
successors.text: Panduranga (Phan Rang and Phan Rí), the last Cham land

ledger.x: 192: Khu Liên rebels against the Han and founds Lâm Ấp at Tượng Lâm.
248: Lâm Ấp seizes most of Rinan.
347: Fan Wen attacks Jin Jiaozhou; Lâm Ấp's frontier is afterwards placed at the Hoành Sơn range.
446: Tan Hezhi's Liu Song army takes and plunders the Lâm Ấp capital.
446: the Song army withdraws with its plunder.
605: Liu Fang's Sui army takes Trà Kiệu.
605: the Sui withdraw.
629: the state calls itself Champa.
757: the Panduranga dynasty takes the throne of Champa.
757: the capital moves south to Virapura near Phan Rang (infobox: Virapura 757–875; Panduranga page: 'established its capital at Virapura, also known as Palai Bachong').
757: the southern coast, Kauthara and Panduranga, is drawn as Champa from the Panduranga dynasty's accession.
758: the Chinese call the state Huanwang (Hoàn Vương).
803: Champa seizes Nghệ An from the Tang.
809: the Tang recover Nghệ An.
875: Indravarman II moves the capital to Indrapura.
982: Lê Hoàn's Vietnamese invasion devastates northern Champa.
982: the court moves south to Vijaya (infobox: Vijaya 982–1471).
989: the end of Lưu Kế Tông's reign at Indrapura ('986–989') closes the Vietnamese presence in the north; the year is the researcher's reading of the reign dates.
1069: Rudravarman III buys his freedom with Địa Lý, Ma Linh and Bố Chính.
1145: Suryavarman II sacks Vijaya and occupies northern Champa.
1149: Jaya Harivarman I retakes Vijaya.
1177: the Cham fleet sacks Angkor.
1181: Jayavarman VII expels the Cham.
1190: a Khmer army under Vidyanandana occupies Vijaya; Panduranga becomes a Khmer vassal.
1191: Vidyanandana turns on his masters.
1192: Jayavarman VII's invasions of Champa begin.
1203: the Khmer conquest completed.
1203: Champa becomes a Khmer province.
1220: the Khmer evacuate Champa.
1283: the Mongols take Vijaya.
1285: the Yuan repelled.
1306: Chế Mân cedes Ô and Lý for Princess Huyền Trân.
1371: Chế Bồng Nga sacks Thăng Long; the war for Hóa Châu, Nghệ An and Thanh Hóa runs to 1390.
1390: Chế Bồng Nga killed.
1402: Indravarman VI cedes Chiêm Động and Cổ Lũy to the Hồ.
1406: the four territories return to Champa as Đại Ngu falls to the Ming.
1470: Lê Thánh Tông's expedition sails.
1471: Vijaya falls.
1471: Champa loses everything north of the Cù Mông Pass.

1471: the Cham court is reduced to Panduranga (infobox: Panduranga polity 1471–1832); two other rulers, 'one in the Central Highlands and one on the coast south of Bình Định', 'subsequently submitted to Thánh Tông as vassals' (1471 war page).
1611: the Nguyễn take Phú Yên, the land between the Cù Mông and Cả passes.
1653: Kauthara lost.
1692: Nguyễn Phúc Chu invades Panduranga.
1694: the Cham prince restored as King of Thuận Thành.
1832: Minh Mạng annexes Panduranga.

wars.name: Fan Wen's war with Jin (347)
wars.outcome: The page records only the attack: 'In 347, king Fan Wen (范文) attacked Jin-controlled Jiaozhou with 40–50,000 troops'; the usual account leaves Lâm Ấp at the Hoành Sơn range.

wars.name: Liu Song campaign against Lâm Ấp (446)
wars.outcome: 'In February 446, the Liu Song dynasty led by Tan Hezhi invaded Lâm Ấp, captured Lâm Ấp's capital'; the capital was plundered and the army withdrew, no border moved.

wars.name: Sui–Lâm Ấp war (605)
wars.outcome: 'In 605 Yang Chien ordered Liu Fang to invade Lâm Ấp'; Trà Kiệu was captured and plundered; the Sui did not stay.

wars.name: Lê Hoàn's invasion of Champa (982)
wars.outcome: 'Lê Hoàn led a Vietnamese invasion that brought mass destruction to northern Champa'; the Vietnamese Lưu Kế Tông reigned at Indrapura 986–989; the Cham court moved to Vijaya.

wars.name: Khmer–Cham wars
wars.outcome: 'lasted from the mid-10th century to the early 13th century'; Champa was a Khmer province from 1203 and 'The conflicts ended after the Khmer army voluntarily retreated from occupying Champa in 1220'.

wars.name: Champa–Đại Việt War (1069)
wars.outcome: Lý Thánh Tông 'burned Vijaya, and captured the king of Champa, Rudravarman III'; the king was released 'in exchange for three areas, known as Địa Lý, Ma Linh, and Bố Chính'.

wars.name: Champa–Đại Việt War (1367–1390)
wars.outcome: 'Champa defensive victory, Vietnamese invasion failed'; 'Status quo ante bellum as no territorial changes; Both states severely weakened'.

wars.name: Champa–Đại Việt War (1471)
wars.outcome: 'Đại Việt victory'; 'Northern Champa (now Quảng Nam, Quảng Ngãi and north of Phú Yên) was annexed to Đại Việt' and 'Champa was reduced to Panduranga'; the border moved 'from Hải Vân Pass to Cù Mông Pass'.

wars.name: Nguyễn conquest of Panduranga (1692–1694)
wars.outcome: 'In 1692, lord Nguyễn Phúc Chu invaded Panduranga, arresting King Po Saut and renaming Panduranga to Trấn Thuận Thành'; after the revolts of 1693–96 the Cham king was restored as 'King of Thuan Thanh' (1694) and 'From 1695 onward, Panduranga had been reduced…

certainty.note: Mandala frontiers; the Hoành Sơn range as the northern limit from the 4th century is a named range, everything else approximate.
The cessions of 1069 (Địa Lý, Ma Linh, Bố Chính) and 1306 (Ô, Lý) are district lines nameable from the pages but not surveyed; the Hải Vân Pass is the northern limit 1306–1470.
The Cù Mông Pass border 1471–1611 and the Cả Pass after 1611 are named lines; Panduranga's limits toward the highlands and toward Nguyễn Bình Thuận after 1695 are approximate.
